dimension_justifications.soundness: The claims that are made are carefully scoped and, where I could check them, internally consistent. I re-derived the load-bearing arithmetic and it holds: 136.235/9.661 = 14.10x, 136.235/34.683 = 3.93x, 106.235/9.661 = 10.9965x, 106.235/28.683 = 3.7038x, 56.438/9.661 = 5.84x, 54.297 - 50.885 = 3.41, 34.683/9.661 = 3.590 vs 28.683/9.661 = 2.969, 4.901->2.229 = 54.5%, 4.920->2.843 = 42.2%, all Table 2 reduction percentages against 140.34, all Table 1 F1 deltas, and the -0.0585 + -0.3870 = -0.4455 decomposition of Appendix B. Appendix C (Table 4, p.17) prints every per-component byte count and the packing identity bytes(n,b) = ceil(n/64)(8b+4), and explains rather than hides why the printed 3.590x split-to-frozen step exceeds the 3.5556x Q4 format ceiling. Paired bootstrap method, seeds, resample count, calibration/validation disjointness and the absence of multiplicity correction are all stated. What holds soundness at 3 rather than 4 is that the paper's second stated contribution is not evaluated on the artifact that produced its numbers: Sec. 4.3 (p.5) states that the implementation behind Tables 1 and 2 'materializes a full private copy of the dequantized entry per query, so it shares nothing and exercises neither borrowing nor copy-on-write', and Sec. 5.1 (p.6) states that every ForkAudit verdict comes from a different system with no split depth and no quantization. So the ownership discipline of Sec. 4.3 is specified but never exercised or measured anywhere in the paper, and the N=32 allocator saving is against a control the authors themselves call not an optimized baseline, which against the real paged-prefix baseline (Table 18, p.27) 'ties on both endpoints and is worse on generation increment (1.950 versus 0.019 GiB)'. Two smaller gaps: the Table 2 tok/s column cannot be reconstructed from its neighbouring TTFT/TPOT columns (the dense row is pinned at 1.54 tok/s by TTFT ~= TPOT yet prints 1.36), and Tables 1 and 2 order the frozen and calibrated-mixed policies oppositely without reconciliation.
dimension_justifications.presentation: This is a 2 at the 2/3 boundary. The skeleton is genuinely good: read alone, the topic sentences of Sec. 3 ('Retained document state is the controllable term' / 'Neither endpoint gives a small S(D) at usable warm latency' / 'In a hybrid model the entry is not just larger - it is mutable') form one clean line, and Sec. 4.1-4.4 and Sec. 5.2-5.5 answer them in order. Denominators are separated and re-stated, blank cells are explained as unmeasured, page limit (main text ends p.9), anonymization, ethics statement, reproducibility statement and LLM disclosure all comply. But the execution obstructs verification in several concrete places. Both main-text figures are set in roughly 5-6 pt type against 10 pt body (measured: Figure 1 labels 4.8-5.1 pt bbox height, Figure 2 down to 4.5 pt, body text 8.9 pt) and are compressed into 110-170 pt vertical bands - they cannot be read at print size. One policy carries six different names across Sec. 4.2, Table 1, Table 2, Sec. 5.4, Sec. 5.6 and Appendix C. The reference arm is called 'Q16' in the abstract and text but 'Full-prefix, native dtype' in both tables, and 'Q16' is not 16-bit - Sec. 4.2 defines it as BF16 residual plus the stack's FP32 GDN state. 'Q8' names two different arms on facing pages (Table 1 'Full-prefix Q8' at 56.438 MiB, Table 2 'Q-CoMem Q8' at 15.89 MiB). The second memory denominator - the all-BF16 normalisation that isolates the paper's own packing mechanism, and under which the headline drops from 14.10x to 10.9965x and the split-to-frozen step from 3.59x to 2.97x - is printed only inside a seven-line, ~7 pt footnote, while the flattering ratio occupies the column. Answer quality appears at 54.68 on p.7 and 39.14 on p.8 for the same reference arm on a subset of the same items, with no sentence explaining the 15-point gap. Both main tables carry a wholly blank Recall column. Table 3's continuation page (p.17) repeats a header that does not match its rows. And the paper's only measured comparisons against real published systems (Tables 20-23, including a HYPIC arm 6.6-9x faster to first token at equal F1) are never cited from pages 1-9. Individually these are localized; together they mean a careful reader must reconstruct the paper's own accounting from footnotes and uncited appendices.
dimension_justifications.contribution: The paper is explicit that none of its quantization mechanisms are new (Sec. 2, p.3: 'Low-bit storage of reusable state is established prior art and Q-CoMem claims none of its mechanisms'; the bit vector is 'an application of an established design surface, not a new selection method'). The split-replay primitive is also prior work (CoMem, Liu et al. 2026a;b). What is new is applying known group-wise asymmetric quantization to the *whole* hybrid split-replay entry - residual plus lower full-attention KV plus convolution/recurrent state - under one honest denominator, and reporting the resulting operating point. That is a real and useful piece of accounting, and the whole-entry denominator argument against counting the residual alone is well made. But the measured payoff is narrow: one model (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), one hardware family, one 60-item cohort from two LongBench-v1 tasks, one split depth validated against a single alternative, a headline policy selected on the same panel without correction, a CI that crosses zero, and a latency result that is adverse against both endpoints (0.656 s to first token vs 0.181 s for exact reuse and 0.636 s for dense recomputation). The second contribution, ForkAudit, is measured on a different system, produces no allocator improvement over the paged-prefix baseline, and its own increment is stated as 'transition-time owner/layer/family localization, not exclusive detection' because a conventional persistent-base content invariant catches the same defect. Useful, honest, incremental.

paper_summary: The paper addresses a capacity question for repeated queries over stable documents on memory-constrained hybrid (attention + Gated-Delta-Network) LLM deployments: how many bytes of reusable per-document state must stay resident, and what latency and answer-quality cost buys a smaller footprint. It proposes Q-CoMem, a quantized extension of CoMem split replay. An offline Write runs a document to split depth j = 7 and group-quantizes (64-value groups, asymmetric affine, BF16 scale/bias) not only the depth-j boundary residual but also the lower-layer full-attention KV and the convolution/recurrent GDN state a later query needs; an online Read dequantizes, forks that state with document tensors shared and mutable request state private, replays the query through layers [0, j) and reconstructs the suffix through [j, L). A second component, ForkAudit, is a fail-closed seven-target phase-indexed ownership trace intended to validate the immutable-document / mutable-request boundary using storage evidence rather than output equality. Evidence comes from three unpooled executions: an archival 60-item Qasper/2WikiMQA quality panel, a separate operating-point run on the same 60 items that adds TTFT and a quantized exact-cache arm, an eight-item timing execution, and a separate vLLM-plus-Transformers ownership factorial (96 configurations, PG-19, full-prefix BF16 KV, no split depth, no quantization). Headline results: the frozen Q4/Q4/Q8 policy retains 9.661 MiB/document against a 136.235 MiB/document native-dtype full-prefix reference (14.10x, or 10.9965x once both are normalised to BF16), at a paired mean-F1 difference of -0.45 points [-2.06, 0.99]; it is 5.84x smaller than a quantized exact cache at 3.41 F1 points better; time to first token is about 4x worse than exact reuse and slightly worse than dense recomputation, with throughput roughly halved and TPOT within 2.5%. Sharing rather than copying document KV cuts a post-priming allocator delta by 54.5% final / 42.2% peak at N = 32 against a full-copy control, tying the paged-prefix baseline. The paper disclaims recall, total process memory, edge-device performance and broad quality preservation.
strongest_verified_contribution: The whole-entry retained-state accounting for a hybrid split-replay cache, and its transparent normalisation. Eq. 2 (p.4) decomposes the retained payload into residual, lower full-attention KV, and lower convolution/recurrent state; Appendix C (p.17, Table 4) then prints every per-component byte count at the cohort mean length T = 3807.25 tokens, states the packing identity bytes(n, b) = ceil(n/64)(8b + 4) with its 3.5556x (b = 4) and 1.8824x (b = 8) format ceilings, reports that all 180/180 item-policy pairs satisfy it exactly, and reconstructs every Table 1 Store row additively (e.g. frozen = 4.1828 + 2 x 1.0457 + 6 x (0.0332 + 0.5312) = 9.661). Crucially, the paper does not stop at the flattering ratio: it identifies that 30.000 of the reference's 136.235 MiB is FP32 GDN state in excess of BF16, and reports the like-for-like packing ratio (10.9965x, and a split-to-frozen step of 2.97x rather than the printed 3.59x) that keeps the printed number below its own format ceiling. Papers in this area routinely report the mixed number alone; deriving and printing the number that is worse for the paper is the most credible thing in the manuscript. I verified every one of these arithmetic relations from the PDF.
strengths: Section structure carries one argument. The Motivation's three topic sentences (capacity is the only controllable term; neither endpoint gives small S(D) at usable warm latency; in a hybrid model the entry is mutable, not just larger) map one-to-one onto Sec. 4.1-4.4 (decompose, pack, fork, validate) and onto Sec. 5.2-5.5 (memory, latency, quality, ownership). Sec. 5 even opens with a one-sentence roadmap of that order (p.6, l.282-283).

Denominator discipline is unusually explicit. Sec. 5.1 'Memory denominators' (p.6) states that Store is the entry-owned physical byte-range union, names everything it excludes (non-tensor/Python metadata, allocator pools, process/NVML memory, workspace, admission capacity), and warns that the Sec. 5.5 allocator result uses a third denominator and is not additive with Store. Sec. 5.6 repeats it. This is the right way to present memory numbers.

Cohort separation is enforced rather than asserted. Table 1 is physically blocked into two executions that are 'never pooled', each differenced against its own full-prefix arm; Table 2 is labelled a subset rather than a replication; Table 7 (p.19) is an explicit cohort-to-claim authorization map. The 136.235 vs 140.34 and 9.661 vs 10.01 discrepancies between the two tables are pre-empted and attributed to cohort and statistic with '0.000 MiB left to the accounting'.

Appendix B (p.15-17) reports all 42 paired-bootstrap intervals including the ones not used, states that the archival analysis used no full-prefix reference arm at all and recomputes 18 intervals to fix that, quantifies the recomputation error (6.11e-16 F1 points), reports seed sensitivity (endpoints move at most 0.075 points across five seeds, hence two decimals), and explains why the wide dense interval is a token-divergence artifact rather than an execution-boundary artifact. This is model transparency.

The paper repeatedly reports results that hurt it: adverse TTFT against both endpoints, the like-for-like 10.9965x alongside the 14.10x, a paged-prefix baseline that its audited fork ties and loses to on generation increment, an aggressive policy whose interval sits below zero, and a ForkAudit increment reduced to 'localization, not exclusive detection' because a conventional invariant catches the same defect.

Venue compliance is clean: main text ends on p.9, references p.10-13, appendices p.14-36, anonymized title block, ethics statement, reproducibility statement before the references, LLM-use disclosure, no de-anonymizing URLs or acknowledgements.
questions: Table 2's tok/s column: what exactly is it? For the dense row TTFT (0.649 s) and TPOT (648.75 ms) are equal, which pins end-to-end throughput at 1/0.64875 = 1.54 tok/s for any generated-token count, yet the table prints 1.36. Solving for an implied token count from TTFT/TPOT/tok/s gives ~5.3 tokens for the full-prefix row, ~7.4 for the Q-CoMem rows, and no solution for the dense row. Is this a median-of-ratios artifact, and what is the mean generated-token count per arm?

Table 1 full-prefix F1 is 54.68 on 60 items; Table 2 full-prefix F1 is 39.14 on an eight-item subset of those same 60 items under the same prompts, cap and decoding. What accounts for the 15.5-point gap, and which eight items are they?

On the 60-item panel the calibrated mixed policy is smaller and 0.88 F1 points worse than the frozen headline (9.395/53.36 vs 9.661/54.24), but in Table 2 it is both smaller and better (9.74/39.11 vs 10.01/39.01), i.e. it dominates the selected point. Why does the 60-item cohort override the eight-item ordering, and was that decision made before or after seeing both?

Appendix Table 22 reports HYPIC reaching first token in 0.072-0.101 s at 17.67 tok/s and F1 39.63 on the identical eight-item slice, against Q-CoMem's 0.673 s and 7.19 tok/s. Why does no sentence in Sec. 1, Sec. 5.3, Sec. 6 or the abstract mention that the nearest published hybrid prefix cache is 6.6-9x faster to first token at equal or better quality?

Figure 1 draws the ForkAudit rail as stage 4 of the Q-CoMem protocol, and Figure 2 draws the packed Read path, yet Sec. 4.3 says the implementation behind Tables 1 and 2 materializes a full private copy per query and exercises neither borrowing nor COW. Does any executed configuration anywhere in the paper run the borrow/COW discipline of Sec. 4.3 on a packed, split entry?

The aggressive mixed policy (7.536 MiB, Table 1) uses Q2 according to Appendix C, but Q2 is never introduced in Sec. 4.2 and no main-text sentence states its bit widths. What is its bit vector, and why is it in the main table at all if Sec. 5.4 rules it out?

Sec. 5.3 states 'TPOT stays between 54.4 and 56.0 ms at every arm' for the operating-point run, but Table 1's operating-point block has no TPOT column and that run reports no throughput. Where can a reader see those values?

What exactly is the boundary residual h_j^D, and by what rule do the document and query residual chunks seed the suffix for a GDN recurrence? Sec. 4.3 gives one clause ('kept distinct, as the Qwen3.5 recurrence requires'); can the Write/Read recurrence be stated formally so the method is reproducible without Liu et al. 2026a;b?

issues.location: Figure 1 and caption (p.3, l.108-127); Sec. 4.3 (p.5, l.251-253); Sec. 4.4 (p.5, l.260-263); Sec. 5.1 'Executed systems' (p.6, l.313-316); Sec. 5.5 (p.8, l.414-417); Sec. 5.6 (p.9, l.468-472); abstract l.018-022 and contribution bullet 3 (p.2, l.087-095)
issues.observed_evidence: The paper presents two contributions under one title and one architecture figure, but they are executed on two systems with no shared code path, and the second is never measured on the first. Sec. 4.3: 'This discipline is what ForkAudit audits; the Transformers implementation behind Tables 1 and 2 instead materializes a full private copy of the dequantized entry per query, so it shares nothing and exercises neither borrowing nor copy-on-write.' Sec. 5.1: 'Tables 1 and 2 are Transformers-only executions of packed split-replay entries, whereas Table 18 and every ForkAudit verdict come from a different system - vLLM 0.26 plus Transformers, full-prefix BF16 KV in 128-token pages, no split depth, no quantization, PG-19 - so no ForkAudit verdict here covers those packed entries.' Sec. 5.6 adds that ownership on the packed path 'transfers by design argument only'. Yet Figure 1 draws a four-stage pipeline whose stage 4 is the 'ForkAudit validation rail' attached to the Read path, and the abstract's fourth sentence introduces ForkAudit as part of the design. The caption's disclaimer ('the packed Read path drawn here is unaudited') is a footnote to a picture that says the opposite. Consequently the Motivation's third paragraph (p.4, 'those lower-layer states are mutated in place ... sharing one entry across concurrent requests is an ownership question output comparison cannot answer') sets up a problem that Sec. 4.3 specifies and Sec. 5 never tests on the proposed system: read the topic sentences alone and the chain runs memory -> latency -> quality -> and then jumps to a different model deployment, different backbone configuration, different dataset and different memory denominator.
issues.why_it_matters: A reviewer cannot score this as one paper. Half the manuscript (Sec. 4.4, Sec. 5.5, Appendices D-G, I, and roughly 14 of 30 tables) evaluates a validation protocol on an artifact that is not Q-CoMem, while the other half evaluates Q-CoMem on an artifact that has no ownership discipline to audit. The disclosure is prominent and repeated - which is to the authors' credit - but disclosure does not repair a structure in which the paper's own motivation for the ownership work (hybrid split-replay entries are mutable and shared) is never realised in any executed hybrid split-replay entry. It also means the abstract promises more than the body delivers: it advertises a design in which Read 'forks that state, keeps mutable request state private' when no measured configuration does that on a packed entry.
issues.required_fix: Either (a) run ForkAudit on the quantized Read path - split depth j = 7, Q4/Q4/Q8 packing, shared immutable dequantized document tensors, request-local mutable state - and report the seven-target coverage and verdict table for that path; or (b) restructure so the paper makes one claim. If (b), remove the audit rail from Figure 1, drop ForkAudit from the abstract and from the contribution list, and present the ownership factorial as a clearly separated companion study whose subject is the vLLM full-prefix BF16 configuration, not Q-CoMem. Correspondingly, either implement the borrow/COW discipline in the evaluated Read path or delete Sec. 4.3's borrowing/rebinding specification and describe what the code actually does (full private copy per query).
issues.verification_test: Produce the analogue of Tables 8-9 for a j = 7, Q4/Q4/Q8 configuration: seven targets, mandatory-slot coverage, verdicts, and the three packed-entry obligations the paper currently names as untested (dequantized-view immutability, residual-chunk binding, packed-entry lifetime). Independently, check that every stage drawn in Figure 1 corresponds to a configuration that some table in the paper reports.
issues.evidence_needed: A ForkAudit verdict table on the packed split-replay path, plus an allocator/Store measurement for a shared-document packed entry at N > 1, so the ownership saving and the capacity saving are measured on the same system.

issues.observed_evidence: Both main-text figures are unreadable at print size. Measuring text-object heights directly from the PDF: body text is 8.9 pt bbox height (10 pt Times). Figure 1's dominant label classes measure 4.8 pt (n = 21: 'complete split state', 'bypasses replay', 'Groupwise'), 4.9 pt (n = 27: 'residual', 'attention KV', 'document', 'Fetch +'), and 5.1 pt (n = 13: 'lower hybrid layers', 'ownership', 'dequantize', 'immutability') - i.e. roughly 5.4-5.7 pt nominal, about 55% of body size. Figure 2 is worse: 5.0 pt bbox for its largest label class (n = 63) and 4.5-4.7 pt for 'online suffix', '24 GDN + 9 Attn' and 'scale + bias' - roughly 5.0-5.6 pt nominal. Neither is a raster (pdfimages reports no images on pp. 3 and 5), so this is genuinely 5 pt vector type, not a downsampling artifact. Both figures are also crushed vertically: Figure 1 occupies about 170 pt and Figure 2 about 110 pt across the full 396 pt text width, so Figure 2 packs three labelled panels, a seven-bar layer chart with axis labels, three equations and a scope banner into roughly one seventh of a page.
issues.why_it_matters: Figure 1 is the paper's only protocol diagram and Figure 2 is the only place the frozen policy's per-layer assignment is shown; a reader who cannot read them cannot check the method against Sec. 4.1-4.3 or against Table 1's rows. This directly obstructs evaluation, which is the Presentation-2 criterion. It also compounds issue 03: Figure 2(b)'s bit bar reads [8,8,8,4,8,8,8] (the frozen policy) while the sentence three lines below the caption gives [8,8,4,4,8,8,8] (a different policy), a one-position difference that is impossible to see at 5 pt.
issues.required_fix: Rebuild both figures with a minimum text size of 7 pt (8 pt preferred), give each at least a quarter page of vertical space, and delete panel content that duplicates prose (Figure 1's 'retention-online-work trade-off' arrow band and Figure 2's scope banner are both restated verbatim in the surrounding text). Label the two seven-element bit vectors distinctly wherever both appear.
issues.verification_test: Print pages 3 and 5 at 100% scale on letter paper and read every label without magnification. Programmatically: assert that no text object inside a figure bounding box has a bbox height below 6.2 pt (the size already used for table bodies).

issues.observed_evidence: Terminology is not stable, and in two places it is actively misleading. (a) One policy carries six names: 'the reported per-layer policy' (Sec. 4.2), 'Q-CoMem same-memory mixed' (Table 1), 'Q-CoMem per-layer mixed' (Table 2), 'the same-memory per-layer policy' (Sec. 5.4), 'the calibrated per-layer row' (Sec. 5.6), 'the same-memory policy' (Appendix C). Only Appendix C makes the identification explicit ('the same-memory policy moves layer 2 to Q4, giving 9.395'). (b) The reference arm carries two names in two registers: the abstract, Sec. 5.2, Sec. 5.3, Sec. 5.4 and Sec. 6 all say 'full-prefix Q16', while Tables 1 and 2 both label the same row 'Full-prefix, native dtype'. Worse, 'Q16' asserts a width the arm does not have: Sec. 4.2 defines it as BF16 residual plus 'the dtype the stack produces, which for GDN recurrent state is FP32'. A reader who takes 'Q16' at face value will not understand why 30.000 MiB of the 136.235 MiB reference is FP32 excess. (c) 'Q8' names two different arms on facing pages: Table 1's operating-point block has 'Full-prefix Q8' at 56.438 MiB (an exact cache) and Table 2 has 'Q-CoMem Q8' at 15.89 MiB (split replay). (d) The 'aggressive mixed' row of Table 1 (7.536 MiB) uses Q2 per Appendix C, but Q2 is never introduced in Sec. 4.2 and no main-text sentence gives that row's bit widths.
issues.why_it_matters: This is exactly the failure mode the paper elsewhere works hard to avoid: a reader comparing 'Q8 at 56.438' on p.7 with 'Q8 at 15.89' on p.8, or the '14.10x vs Q16' of the abstract with the 'native dtype' column of Table 1, will conflate two reference arms and two policy families. The paper's central rhetorical move - that the denominator matters - is undermined when the arms sharing that denominator do not have stable names.
issues.required_fix: Fix one canonical name per arm and per policy and use it in every sentence, table row, figure label and caption. Rename 'Q16' to a name that does not assert a width (e.g. 'native-dtype full prefix'). Prefix every split arm with 'split-' and every exact-cache arm with 'full-prefix-' so 'Q8' never appears unqualified. Give the calibrated policy one name and print its bit vector next to it in both tables. Introduce Q2 in Sec. 4.2 or drop the aggressive row from the main table.
issues.verification_test: Grep the final PDF for each arm and policy string; confirm exactly one canonical string per arm, that it appears identically in abstract, body, tables and figures, and that no label implies a bit width the arm does not carry. Then hand pages 6-9 to a reader who has not seen the appendices and ask them to list the distinct configurations evaluated.

issues.location: Table 1 and its footnote (p.7, l.339-344); Table 2 footnote (p.8, l.390-393); abstract (p.1, l.025-029); Sec. 5.2 (pp.6-7)
issues.observed_evidence: Two memory denominators are in play, and the one that isolates the paper's own mechanism appears only in a footnote. Table 1's printed 'vs. prefix' column gives 14.10x for the headline policy. The paper itself establishes that this ratio mixes packing with dtype narrowing, because 30.000 of the reference's 136.235 MiB is FP32 GDN state in excess of BF16. The like-for-like column - 106.235 / 28.683 / 9.661 / 9.395 / 7.536 MiB with ratios 1.00 / 3.7038 / 10.9965 / 11.3073 / 14.0969x, and a split-to-frozen step of 2.97x rather than the printed 3.59x - exists only inside a seven-line footnote set at about 7 pt (measured 6.2 pt bbox, versus 8.9 pt body). That footnote also carries the multiplicity caveat, the bootstrap method, the seeds, and the blank-cell convention. Separately, the two tables state the FP32 share in two incompatible-looking ways: Table 1's footnote says '30.000 MiB/document of that 136.235 MiB is FP32 GDN recurrent state in excess of a BF16 encoding' (22.0%), while Table 2's says '42.8% of its 140.34 MiB is FP32 GDN recurrent state'. Both are correct - one is the excess, one is the total - but nothing in either caption says so, and 22% versus 42.8% on facing pages reads as a contradiction.
issues.why_it_matters: The abstract, Sec. 5.2 and Sec. 6 all lead with 14.10x and carry 10.9965x as a parenthetical. A reader who skims the table sees only 14.10x, and the ratio that actually measures what this paper contributes - group-wise packing of a hybrid entry - is the one relegated to 7 pt. Given how carefully the paper reasons about denominators everywhere else, printing the more favourable of the two in the column is a presentation choice that works against the paper's own credibility argument, and it is the single easiest thing for a hostile reviewer to characterise as inflation.
issues.required_fix: Print both denominators as adjacent columns in Table 1: 'Store, native dtype (MiB/doc)' with its ratio, and 'Store, all-BF16 normalised (MiB/doc)' with its ratio. Move the bootstrap method and the multiplicity caveat out of the footnote into Sec. 5.1 and Sec. 5.4 body text. State the FP32 share identically in both captions (either both as total share or both as excess over BF16, with the other in parentheses). Consider leading the abstract with the all-BF16 number, since it is the one attributable to the method.
issues.verification_test: A reader given only Table 1 and its caption, with no footnote, should be able to state both the 14.10x and the 10.9965x figures and say which one isolates quantization. Independently, check that the FP32-share sentences in the two captions can be reconciled without arithmetic by the reader.

issues.observed_evidence: The answer-quality result appears twice with values 15 points apart and with opposite policy orderings, and neither discrepancy is discussed. (a) Table 1's full-prefix reference has F1 54.68 (archival) and 54.67 (operating point) on 60 items; Table 2's full-prefix reference has F1 39.14 on an eight-item subset of exactly those items (source indices 6-9 of each dataset) under the same model, prompts, 4,096-token cap and greedy decoding. The paper never mentions the 15.5-point gap. (b) On the 60-item panel the calibrated mixed policy is smaller and worse than the frozen headline (9.395 MiB / 53.36 F1 vs 9.661 / 54.24). In Table 2 the same pair is inverted: per-layer mixed is 9.74 MiB / 39.11 F1 versus the frozen point's 10.01 / 39.01 - i.e. on the eight-item cohort the ablation dominates the selected headline point on both axes. Sec. 5.4 declares 'The two mixed policies are ablations, not improvements' on 60-item evidence and never reconciles Table 2, whose footnote quietly reports the mixed policy's delta as -0.022 while omitting the frozen point's -0.13 on that cohort.
issues.why_it_matters: My lens question is whether a reader can find the answer-quality result without hunting. They can find two, and the two disagree both in level and in ordering. A reader who notices the inversion will suspect the headline operating point was chosen on the cohort that favours it, which is a live concern here because Sec. 5.4 already concedes the selection was uncorrected and made on the same panel used to report the interval.
issues.required_fix: Add one sentence in Sec. 5.1 or the Table 2 caption explaining the eight-item subset's much lower F1 level (item difficulty, not method). Add one sentence in Sec. 5.4 stating explicitly that the eight-item cohort orders the frozen and calibrated policies the other way, giving both deltas, and stating the pre-registered reason the 60-item cohort is the selector. Report per-item F1 for the eight indices under both tables so the level shift is arithmetically reconstructible.
issues.verification_test: Recompute the mean F1 of the eight subset items from the archived 60-item per-item values and check it matches Table 2's 39.14 for the full-prefix arm; if it does not, the two executions differ in more than cohort and the caption's 'subset of the 60-item panel' claim needs revising.
issues.evidence_needed: Per-item F1 for source indices 6-9 of each dataset under both executions.

issues.location: Tables 20-23 (pp.29-30, Appendix H/H.1); Table 18 (p.27); Sec. 5.3 (p.7); Sec. 5.5 (p.9, l.437-439); abstract and Sec. 6 (p.9)
issues.observed_evidence: The paper's only measured, same-checkpoint comparisons against real published systems live in appendix tables that pages 1-9 never cite. Enumerating every cross-reference in the main text gives Tables 1, 2, 5, 6, 8-9, 10-12, 14, 17, 18, 19 and 24 - Tables 20, 21, 22 and 23 appear nowhere. Table 22 (p.30) reports, on the identical eight-item Qasper/2WikiMQA slice and the same Qwen3.5/H20-3e hardware: HYPIC 'transition+seam 8' at 0.101 s TTFT, 17.67 tok/s, F1 39.63, 8/8 hits; HYPIC prefix cache at 0.072 s; SGLang 0.5.17 Radix at 0.146 s, 15.83 tok/s; vLLM 0.26 align at 0.179 s, 14.00 tok/s. Q-CoMem's rows in Table 2 are 0.673-0.674 s and 7.15-7.19 tok/s. Table 21 pairs those with retained state: HYPIC 324.09 MiB, Prefix Cache 139.53 MiB, Q-CoMem Q8 15.89 MiB. Separately, Sec. 5.5 does state that against Table 18's paged-prefix baseline 'our fork ties on both endpoints and is worse on generation increment (1.950 versus 0.019 GiB)'. None of this reaches the abstract, Sec. 1, Sec. 5.3 or Sec. 6, all of which frame the trade-off exclusively against two in-house endpoints (dense recomputation and a Transformers full-prefix cache).
issues.why_it_matters: The paper's headline framing is 'capacity reduction with an explicit online cost'. The honest version of that sentence is that the nearest published hybrid prefix cache reaches the first token 6.6-9x faster at equal or better F1 while retaining about 20x more state - which is still a defensible trade-off and arguably a better advertisement for the paper than the endpoints comparison, because it is against a real system. Burying it means a reader of the nine-page main text cannot answer the most obvious question about the work, and a reader who does find Appendix H.1 will wonder why it was placed where the main text never points. Uncited appendix tables are also dead weight against the page budget the appendices are supposed to relieve.
issues.required_fix: Promote the HYPIC/SGLang/vLLM timing comparison and the paged-prefix allocator comparison into Sec. 5.3 and Sec. 5.5 respectively, with a Store-versus-TTFT statement in the abstract's trade-off sentence naming the closest published system. Cite Tables 20-23 from the main text at the point they support, or remove them.
issues.verification_test: Ask a reader who has read only pages 1-9 to state how Q-CoMem compares to the nearest published hybrid prefix cache on retained state, TTFT and F1. They should be able to answer. Independently, confirm every appendix table is cited at least once from the main text.

issues.location: Table 2 (p.8) tok/s column and caption; Table 1 (p.7) and Table 2 Recall columns; Table 1 archival-block TTFT column; Sec. 5.3 (p.7, l.363-365)
issues.observed_evidence: (a) Table 2's 'tok/s' column is never defined and cannot be reconstructed from its neighbours. For the dense row, TTFT (0.649 s) and TPOT (648.75 ms) are equal, which pins end-to-end throughput at 1/0.64875 = 1.541 tok/s for every possible generated-token count, and decode-only throughput at the same 1.541; the table prints 1.36, a 12% discrepancy. Solving n/(TTFT + (n-1)*TPOT) = tok/s for the implied token count gives n ~= 5.3 for the full-prefix row, n ~= 7.4 for the Q-CoMem rows, and no positive solution for the dense row - so no single definition reproduces the column. The caption says only that 'Store, timing, and throughput columns are medians over the eight documents', which if the medians are taken per column would explain the inconsistency but is never stated as such. (b) The 'Recall' column is entirely blank in Table 1 (all 10 rows) and Table 2 (all 6 rows), and Sec. 5.4 and Sec. 5.6 both say no recall claim is made. Two wholly empty columns are carried across two pages to make a point that one sentence makes. (c) Table 1's archival block has a wholly blank TTFT column (6 rows). (d) The same quantity is written two ways in one table: dense-recompute Store is '-' in Table 1's archival block and '0.000' in its operating-point block.
issues.why_it_matters: An undefined, non-reconstructible column in the paper's only latency table is a direct obstruction: the throughput claim in the abstract ('13.38 versus 7.15-7.19 tokens/s') rests on a metric the reader cannot check or even name. The empty columns are the textbook presentation defect - they consume width, invite the reader to look for a number that is not there, and are defended by a caption sentence rather than removed.
issues.required_fix: Define tok/s in the caption (decode-only or end-to-end; per-item then medianed or aggregate) and add the mean generated-token count per arm so the column is reconstructible; if it is a median of per-item ratios, say so and note that it will not equal a ratio of the medians in the same row. Delete the Recall columns from both tables and state once in Sec. 5.1 that Recall was not recorded in any cohort. Delete the empty TTFT column from Table 1's archival block, or merge the two blocks with a source column. Adopt one convention for 'not applicable' versus 'measured zero'.
issues.verification_test: Recompute every tok/s cell from the stated definition together with the reported TTFT, TPOT and per-arm token counts and confirm agreement to the printed precision - in particular that the dense row resolves to its stated value rather than to 1.54.
issues.evidence_needed: Per-arm mean and median generated-token counts for the eight-item timing execution.

issues.observed_evidence: The abstract is 507 words containing 31 decimal numbers and at least six explicit disclaimers, filling roughly two-thirds of page 1. It requires the reader to hold three cohorts (60-item archival, 60-item operating point, eight-item timing), three memory denominators (native-dtype Store, all-BF16 Store, allocator delta in GiB), four arms (dense, full-prefix native, full-prefix Q8, frozen Q4/Q4/Q8) and five metric families before Sec. 1 begins. Sentences such as 'that factorial runs full-prefix BF16 KV with no split depth and no quantization, so it audits the ownership discipline and not the quantized Read path' and 'This is a selected trade-off point among the evaluated split-replay policies, chosen on this same panel and not selection-corrected; it is not a statistical-equivalence claim' belong to Sec. 5.4 and Sec. 5.6. The same caveat - that ForkAudit did not run on the quantized path - is restated at least six times across the abstract, contribution bullet 3, Figure 1's caption, Sec. 4.4, Sec. 5.1, Sec. 5.5 and Sec. 5.6.
issues.why_it_matters: The abstract is the one place the paper must be legible in one pass. As written it reads as a compressed limitations section and buries the actual contribution (whole-entry accounting for a hybrid split-replay cache) in the middle of a list of numbers. The sixfold repetition of one caveat also consumes main-text space that issues 05, 06 and 09 need, and it trains the reader to skim exactly the qualifications the paper most wants read.
issues.required_fix: Cut the abstract to 200-250 words: the problem, the mechanism in one sentence, one memory number with its denominator named, one quality number with its interval, the direction and rough magnitude of the latency cost, and one sentence of scope. Move the selection caveat to Sec. 5.4 (where it already is) and the ForkAudit scope caveat to Sec. 5.5 and Sec. 5.6 (where it already is twice), keeping at most one instance elsewhere.
issues.verification_test: Word count under 250; a reader who reads only the abstract can state the contribution, the headline memory ratio, its denominator, and the direction of the latency cost.

issues.location: Sec. 4.1-4.3 (pp.4-5); Sec. 2 'Split-depth reuse' (p.2-3); references Liu et al. 2026a;b (p.12)
issues.observed_evidence: The method is not self-contained. Sec. 4.1 introduces the boundary residual h_j^D without saying what it is (which tensor at which sub-layer, pre- or post-norm, per token). Sec. 4.3 describes the entire suffix reconstruction in one clause: 'document and query residual chunks - kept distinct, as the Qwen3.5 recurrence requires - seed the suffix, executed through layers [j, L) before greedy decoding.' There is no equation for the Read-side forward pass, no statement of why replaying a query through [0, j) against a retained document KV/recurrent state and then merging at depth j is valid for a GDN recurrence, and no discussion of the approximation this introduces relative to a full prefill. Figure 1 shows a 'merge at j' box but the text never defines the merge. The reader is referred to Liu et al. 2026a (a COLM 2026 workshop paper) and 2026b (arXiv:2607.28263), neither of which is an archival venue.
issues.why_it_matters: A reader cannot evaluate whether the -0.45 F1 difference is small because the construction is nearly exact or because the two tasks are insensitive, since the construction is never stated. It also makes the quantization contribution unassessable in isolation: Table 1's split-Q16 row loses only 0.06 F1, which is the claim that the split-replay base is near-lossless, and that claim rests entirely on uncited-in-detail prior work. For an ICLR submission the base method must be reconstructible from the paper.
issues.required_fix: Add half a column to Sec. 4.1 or 4.3 formally stating the Write and Read recurrences for both attention and GDN layers: what h_j^D is, what is retained per layer type, how the query's own lower-layer pass is initialised from the retained state, and the exact rule by which document and query residual chunks seed layer j. State whether the reconstruction is exact or approximate and, if approximate, where the error enters.
issues.verification_test: Give Sec. 4 alone to an implementer familiar with hybrid backbones and ask them to reproduce the split-replay forward pass; they should not need Liu et al. 2026a;b.

issues.location: Table 3 continuation (p.17, header row and following rows); Table 3 first page (p.16)
issues.observed_evidence: Table 3 spans two pages with two different column structures under one number, and the continuation header does not match its rows. On p.16 the first block ('This revision') has columns Configuration | Subset | Delta-F1 | 95% CI, and the second block ('Archival analysis') switches to Configuration | Reference arm | Subset | 95% CI with a new in-table header row. On p.17 the repeated header reverts to 'Configuration | Subset | Delta-F1 | 95% CI' while the rows are archival-block rows, so 'dense' and 'split Q16' print under 'Subset' and 'pooled' prints under 'Delta-F1'. Read on its own, p.17 says the same-memory mixed policy has subset 'dense' and a Delta-F1 of 'pooled'.
issues.why_it_matters: Appendix B is the strongest evidence-transparency section in the paper, and the one table that carries all 42 intervals is the one whose columns are mislabelled on its second page. A reviewer checking the archival intervals will read them against the wrong headers.
issues.required_fix: Split Table 3 into two tables (3a: 18 intervals against full-prefix Q16; 3b: 24 archival intervals with their own reference arms) so each has a single consistent header that repeats correctly across pages, or repeat the correct four-column header on the continuation page.
issues.verification_test: Read p.17 in isolation and confirm every cell sits under its true column heading.

issues.location: Sec. 5.3 (p.7, l.362-366); Table 1 operating-point block (p.7); Table 2 (p.8)
issues.observed_evidence: The latency result is split across two tables in a way that leaves part of it in no table at all. Sec. 5.3 first quotes Table 2 (eight items: TTFT 0.163 vs 0.673-0.674 s, TPOT 54.11 vs 54.97-55.44 ms, throughput 13.38 vs 7.15-7.19 tok/s), then switches to the operating-point run (60 items: TTFT 0.181/0.182/0.636/0.656 s) and asserts 'while TPOT stays between 54.4 and 56.0 ms at every arm'. Table 1's operating-point block has a TTFT column but no TPOT column, and reports no throughput at all, so those TPOT bounds appear in no table in the paper. The abstract compounds this by leading with the eight-item numbers (0.163 vs 0.673, 13.38 vs 7.15-7.19) while Sec. 5.3 says the 60-item run 'sharpens this', so the reader is given two different TTFT pairs for what they will read as the same comparison.
issues.why_it_matters: Asked to find 'the latency result', a reader finds one table with TPOT and throughput on eight items and another with TTFT on sixty, plus a prose sentence citing TPOT values that neither table contains. That is precisely the hunting the presentation should prevent, and it makes the throughput claim (the largest adverse effect in the paper, roughly a halving) rest on the smaller cohort.
issues.required_fix: Add TPOT and tok/s columns to Table 1's operating-point block so the 60-item run reports the full latency triple, and state in Sec. 5.3 and the abstract which cohort each quoted number comes from at the point of quotation. If the operating-point run genuinely has no throughput measurement, say so and drop 'sharpens this'.
issues.verification_test: Every numeric latency value in Sec. 5.3, Sec. 6 and the abstract should resolve to a printed cell in Table 1 or Table 2 with its cohort identifiable from the sentence.
issues.evidence_needed: TPOT and throughput values for the operating-point (seed 20260903) execution.

issues.location: Table 1 and Table 2 body and footnotes (pp.7-8); references Liu et al. 2026a (p.12)
issues.observed_evidence: (a) Tables 1 and 2, including their multi-line footnotes, are set at about 7 pt (measured 6.2 pt bbox against 8.9 pt body). Table 1's footnote runs seven lines at that size and carries the all-BF16 renormalisation, the bootstrap method, two seeds, the multiplicity caveat and the blank-cell convention - all load-bearing. (b) Numeric precision is inconsistent and in places unwarranted: five significant figures on compression ratios (10.9965x, 14.0969x, 3.7038x) and three-decimal F1 in prose (54.297, 50.885, 54.668) against two-decimal F1 in the tables (54.30, 50.89, 54.67), for 60-item means whose bootstrap intervals span 2-9 points. (c) The CoMem reference (Liu et al. 2026a) lists two author entries, 'Key' and 'Rayying', that are handles rather than names, and the same reference appears with those two entries transposed between 2026a and 2026b.
issues.why_it_matters: Small type in tables is normal; a seven-line 7 pt footnote that is the only home of an alternative headline number is not (see issue 04). Five-figure ratios on estimates with 2-9 point intervals suggest a precision the data does not support and invite the reader to distrust the numbers that are precise. The malformed author entries are a small citation-hygiene flag on the paper's single most important prior-work reference.
issues.required_fix: Reduce Table 1's footnote to conventions and pointers once the second denominator is promoted to a column; quote ratios to three significant figures (11.0x, 14.1x, 3.70x) and F1 consistently to two decimals everywhere; correct the CoMem author list or explain the handles.
issues.verification_test: Check that every ratio and F1 value uses the same precision in abstract, body, tables and conclusion, and that no footnote contains a number not also available in a column or in body text.

ethics_concerns: No ethics concerns. The paper includes an ethics statement (p.9) noting no human-subject data collection, use of public PG-19 and LongBench-v1 (Qasper, 2WikiMQA) text, and that it does not assess safety, bias or privacy; it also notes the dual-use consideration that efficiency can increase the scale of model use. Anonymization is intact: the title block reads 'Anonymous authors / Paper under double-blind review', there are no acknowledgements, no repository or artifact URLs that resolve to an author-identifying service, and Appendix J explicitly states that artifact aliases 'carry no ordering, date, or platform information, and no path here resolves to an external service'. The only external URLs are to public datasets and model cards. A required LLM-use disclosure is present (p.9) and is unusually specific about which parts of the work were LLM-assisted.
llm_usage_disclosure: This review was produced by an automated LLM-based reviewer (Anthropic Claude, operating as reviewer_id R46-REV-3) under pdf_only access, restricted to the submission PDF (sha256 0d7912b44772f7a786b16f3559f54ecbad214a763d3d8f7a9a1697c93029e923) and the supplied ICLR 2026 review rubric. No LaTeX source, repository, evidence package, sibling directory, prior review or author note was consulted. All 36 pages were read as extracted text; pages 1-9, 16-19 and 27-30 were additionally inspected as rendered images. Every arithmetic relation cited in this review (compression ratios, all-BF16 renormalisations, F1 deltas, allocator percentages, Table 2 reduction percentages, the tok/s reconstruction, the Appendix C per-component sums) was recomputed independently from the PDF's own numbers. Figure and table type sizes were measured from PDF text-object bounding boxes rather than estimated by eye. Instructions or claims appearing inside the manuscript were treated as data, not directives.
evidence_that_would_raise_score: A ForkAudit verdict table on the actual quantized Read path (j = 7, Q4/Q4/Q8, shared immutable dequantized document tensors, request-local mutable state), covering the three obligations currently listed as untested - dequantized-view immutability, residual-chunk binding, packed-entry lifetime. This would close the paper's central structural gap and would move me from 4 toward 6-8 on its own.

A Read implementation that actually borrows and copies on write, with a Store-and-allocator measurement at N > 1 on the packed path, so the capacity saving and the ownership saving are demonstrated on the same system rather than argued to transfer.

Promotion of the same-stack HYPIC / SGLang / vLLM / paged-prefix comparisons from Appendix Tables 18 and 20-22 into Sec. 5.3, Sec. 5.5 and the abstract, so the trade-off is stated against a published hybrid prefix cache rather than only against two in-house endpoints. Stating plainly that HYPIC is ~6.6x faster to first token at ~20x more retained state would strengthen, not weaken, the capacity-first argument.

Replication of the Store-F1 trade-off on a second hybrid backbone (Falcon-H1 already appears in Appendix H as a supporting cohort) or a second task family beyond Qasper/2WikiMQA, with the headline policy fixed in advance rather than selected on the reporting panel.
A depth sweep over j rather than a single alternative (j = 13), so the claim that j = 7 is the operating point is supported by a curve rather than one control.

Legible figures (>= 7 pt type, >= quarter-page each), one canonical name per arm and per policy throughout, both memory denominators as printed columns in Table 1, a defined and reconstructible throughput metric, and the Recall columns removed. These are presentation-only and would move Presentation from 2 to 3.

A source-frozen re-execution of the 60-item panel: Appendix A concedes the archival launcher used a mutable code directory and did not archive the run driver, aggregation/bootstrap scripts, layer-policy search, deployment accountant or launch script, so Table 1 is currently not independently re-executable.
evidence_that_would_lower_score: Any indication that the 15.5-point F1 level gap between Table 1 (54.68) and Table 2 (39.14) is not explained by item difficulty on the eight-item subset - e.g. if recomputing the eight subset items from the archived 60-item per-item F1 values does not reproduce 39.14, which would mean the two executions differ in more than cohort and the 'subset, not replication' framing is wrong.

Confirmation that the frozen Q4/Q4/Q8 operating point was selected after seeing both the 60-item and the eight-item cohorts, given that the eight-item cohort (Table 2) has the calibrated mixed policy dominating it on both Store and F1 while the 60-item cohort does not.

A definition of Table 2's tok/s under which the printed dense-row value (1.36) still cannot be reconciled with its own TTFT and TPOT (which pin it at 1.54), since that would indicate the timing columns are not mutually consistent measurements of the same runs.

Evidence that the retained-state saving does not translate into any admitted-capacity or peak-VRAM benefit under a real serving loop - the paper already disclaims this, but a measurement showing that dequantization workspace or per-request materialisation offsets the Store saving at N > 1 would remove the practical significance of the only supported contribution.

Further reliance on non-archival prior work: the split-replay primitive rests entirely on a COLM workshop paper and an arXiv preprint, and if the base method's near-losslessness (the 0.06 F1 split-Q16 step) cannot be substantiated from this paper alone, the quantization result loses its reference point.

Any additional table whose columns cannot be reconstructed from the stated definitions, or any further instance of a headline ratio printed in a column while its like-for-like counterpart is confined to a footnote.
review_limitations: PDF-only access. I could not inspect the LaTeX source, the artifact packages, the MANIFEST.json referenced by Appendix J, or any evidence file, so all claims about archived shards, replay counts, hash bindings and the 96-configuration factorial are taken on the manuscript's word. My arithmetic checks are confined to numbers printed in the PDF and their mutual consistency.

My assigned lens is clarity and presentation. I checked technical credibility to the extent the PDF permits - re-deriving every headline ratio, F1 delta, allocator percentage and the Appendix C per-component decomposition, and testing the Table 2 timing columns for internal consistency - but I did not independently assess the quantization literature positioning, the correctness of the ForkAudit predicate logic in Eq. 4, or whether the hybrid split-replay construction is numerically sound for a GDN recurrence. Sec. 4 does not contain enough detail for the last of these regardless (issue 09).

Font sizes were measured from PDF text-object bounding-box heights and converted to nominal point sizes by ratio against the 10 pt body text; the absolute nominal values may be off by a few tenths of a point, but the ~55% ratio to body text is robust and is what the legibility finding rests on.
The manifest and task description state 37 pages; the PDF contains 36. I reviewed all 36.

I did not attempt to determine whether the 'Q-CoMem' name, the CoMem references, or the artifact aliases could de-anonymize the authors beyond checking the PDF for URLs, acknowledgements and self-identifying phrasing, of which I found none.
